passage: Dear Tejas, Week two in Kyoto and I have learnt more from asking than from any guidebook. On day one I nearly handed my host a gift with one hand, until Emi, the assistant, smiled and showed me she uses both hands. I asked what to wear to the tea house, and Emi said plain clothes, covered shoulders and clean socks, since shoes come off. At the office nobody expected me to bow perfectly, but they seemed to like that I tried. I stopped assuming a short answer meant coldness; Emi told me it is just her way of being polite. Last night my host invited me home for dinner. My whole lesson: ask before you guess. Write soon. Manoj

qa.q: Who showed Manoj how to hand over the gift?
qa.a: Emi showed Manoj that both hands are used.

qa.q: What is Manoj feeling toward the people in Kyoto?
qa.a: Warmth and curiosity; Manoj is grateful for Emi's help and pleased to be invited to dinner.

qa.q: What habit prevented errors for Manoj?
qa.a: Asking locals before guessing at what a greeting, gift or answer means.

qa.q: How might Emi have felt seeing Manoj ask about clothes and gifts?
qa.a: Pleased and respected, since Emi smiled and helped and did not seem to mind the questions.

grounding: A traveller asks locals about gifts, dress and manners before assuming meaning, and is welcomed with warmth.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Thanks for having me, Alka. I'm Ankita, and my first week in Bali was all about asking. I didn't want to assume anything. Wayan, who runs my guesthouse, told me that at the temple I'd need a sarong and sash, and to hand things over with my right hand. I asked about the little offerings on the pavement, and Wayan laughed and said people usually step around them. I was so afraid of causing offence that I asked everything: how to greet people, what to bring if a family invites you to a ceremony. Wayan said a small gift of fruit was fine. By the end of the week I was invited to eat with the family. Curiosity opens doors faster than confidence.

qa.q: What did Wayan say Ankita would need at the temple?
qa.a: Wayan said Ankita would need a sarong and sash.

qa.q: Why did Ankita ask so many questions, and how did it feel?
qa.a: Ankita feared causing offence and wanted to understand instead of assume, so it felt nervous but eager.

qa.q: What would you advise a traveller arriving in a new country?
qa.a: Ask locals about greetings, gifts and dress before assuming meaning, and stay curious.

qa.q: How might Wayan have felt about Ankita's questions?
qa.a: Welcomed and respected, judging by the laugh and the invitation to eat with the family.

grounding: A traveller asks a local about greetings, gifts and dress before assuming meaning, and wins warmth.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
I'm Zubin, and I shared a desk with Ojas the month before our firm posted us both to Nairobi. What I saw was this: while I read travel blogs and assumed, Ojas asked. Every evening he messaged Wanjiru, a Kenyan colleague from the video calls, with small questions. How do people greet elders? Is it rude to refuse tea? Which hand do you use to give something? What should I bring when invited home? He wrote her answers in a little notebook. I teased him about it.
In Nairobi, at Wanjiru's family lunch, her grandmother held out her hand. Ojas took it in both of his, dipped his head, and gave the gift, a box of sweets, with his right hand. She said something in Kikuyu and everyone laughed warmly. I was standing there with my phone, not knowing what to do. I can't say what he felt. He looked calm.

qa.q: Where did Ojas write down Wanjiru's answers?
qa.a: In a little notebook.

qa.q: What might Ojas have been feeling at Wanjiru's family lunch, and what suggests it?
qa.a: He seemed calm and at ease; his steady greeting, taking the grandmother's hand in both of his, suggests his preparation made him feel confident.

qa.q: What did Ojas's approach get right that Zubin's did not?
qa.a: Ojas asked a local person about greetings, tea and gifts instead of assuming from blogs, so he knew how to show respect when it mattered.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru's grandmother have seen Ojas?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and warmed by a guest who greeted her properly, which is why the family laughed kindly.

grounding: It illustrates a worker who asks locals about greetings, gifts and customs before arriving, and how curiosity and humility win warmth.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
Week one: Lalit landed in Jakarta for his new job and, before accepting any invitations, bought coffee for Pak Budi, the office driver who had lived there all his life. "What should I know?" he asked. Budi explained: shoes off at the door, give and take with the right hand, don't touch anyone's head, and bring something small, like fruit. Lalit wrote it on his phone. His friend Madhav, on a call from Pune, laughed: "Just be yourself, yaar."
Week three: Lalit's manager invited him home. He took off his shoes, handed over a basket of mangosteens with his right hand, and when the youngest child ran up, he smiled rather than patting her head. The grandmother told him he was "sopan", polite, and gave him extra rice.
Week five: Budi's daughter got married, and Lalit was invited. Madhav, hearing this, said, "How are you already on wedding lists?"

qa.q: What did Lalit bring to his manager's home?
qa.a: A basket of mangosteens, handed over with his right hand.

qa.q: How did Lalit probably feel when the grandmother called him polite?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and relieved that his careful questions had paid off and he was welcomed.

qa.q: Why was asking Pak Budi a wise first step?
qa.a: Budi had lived there all his life and could explain real customs like shoes, right hand and heads, so Lalit could avoid mistakes rather than guess.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Lalit's approach by week five?
qa.a: Madhav first laughed at the preparation, but by week five he seems surprised and a little impressed that Lalit is already invited to a wedding.

grounding: It illustrates a worker who asks a local about greetings, gifts and taboos before assuming meaning, and wins warmth over time.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Vijay, you're off to Osaka next month, so let your Mridul sir tell you one old story before you pack. I was twenty-four, sent there for a project, and I thought I knew everything. On my first day a colleague gave me his card with both hands and a little bow. I nearly took it with one hand and stuffed it in my back pocket, as I did in Delhi. But something made me stop and ask the receptionist, Mrs Tanaka, what to do. She showed me: two hands, read it, keep it on the table in the meeting. She also told me not to write names in red ink. I asked her questions every day for a month. When I left, the team gave me a farewell dinner, and Mrs Tanaka cried. Imagine. I still have that colleague's card.

qa.q: Who did young Mridul ask about the card?
qa.a: He asked the receptionist, Mrs Tanaka.

qa.q: What made young Mridul stop before pocketing the card?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a little cautious, sensing he might not understand the custom, and chose to ask instead of assuming.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mridul's story?
qa.a: Stopping to ask Mrs Tanaka instead of doing it the Delhi way, which started a month of daily questions and built real warmth with the team.

qa.q: How might Mrs Tanaka have felt about the young visitor who kept asking?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and fond of him, since his questions showed care, which is why she cried at his farewell.

grounding: It illustrates a young worker abroad who asks locals about greetings and customs before assuming, and whose humility wins warmth.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The naming ceremony started at eight, and at seven Irawati was still ironing a kurta in her rented room in Kumasi. Jyoti, her flatmate, was already at the door. "Just wear anything and take a box of sweets, it's fine." Irawati hesitated. At an office party last month she had held out her left hand to shake and watched a colleague's smile freeze. She knocked on her landlady's door instead. "Auntie Ama, quick question. Three, actually." Ama laughed and counted on her fingers: greet the elders first, use the right hand only, and a small gift for the baby is kinder than sweets. "And that colour is good. Not black, that is for funerals." They reached twenty minutes late, but Irawati went straight to the grandmother first, right hand held out. The old woman took it in both of hers and pulled Irawati down to a seat in the front row.

qa.q: Whose door did Irawati knock on before the ceremony?
qa.a: She knocked on her landlady's door and asked Auntie Ama.

qa.q: Why did Irawati hesitate when Jyoti told her to wear anything and take sweets?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and cautious, because she remembered a colleague's smile freezing when she offered her left hand, and she did not want to cause offence again.

qa.q: Which choice paid off at the ceremony, and why?
qa.a: Taking a few minutes to ask Auntie Ama, even though it made them late, meant Irawati greeted the grandmother first with her right hand and was welcomed to a front seat.

qa.q: How might the grandmother at the ceremony see Irawati?
qa.a: She likely saw a newcomer who had bothered to learn their ways and showed respect, which is why she held Irawati's hand in both of hers.

grounding: Shows a worker abroad asking a local about greetings, gifts and dress before assuming, and the warmth that humility wins.
